newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 8.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- INFLATION FEARS AS SALES JUMP

Figures from the Confederation of British Industry for high street sales during the month of October reveal the fastest rate of increase since 1988, prompting concern about inflationary pressures. The news is expected to increase pressure on the chancellor to increase interest rates again at some point before the next general election. The Bank of England earlier in the week warned that such action would be required if government inflation targets were to be met.
-- CALENERGY LIFTS NORTHERN ELECTRIC STAKE

The US power company CalEnergy has managed to increase its stake in bid target Northern Electric to 26.8 percent after taking advantage of a fall in equity prices in the sector to snap up a further 1.35 million shares. The fall in the sector occurred after it was revealed that Dominion Resources, another US energy company, was considering making a takeover bid for East Midlands Electricity.
-- MMC TO PROBE PACKAGE HOLIDAY GROUPS

The Monopolies & Mergers Commission is to launch an investigation into Britain's holiday trade amid concerns that the dominance of some package holiday companies is limiting the scope of consumer choice. The investigation will concentrate in particular on the relationship between package holiday firms and subsidiary retail travel outlets to determine whether or not such link-ups have resulted in anti-competitive behaviour such as the selling of cheaper holidays only to those agreeing to purchase insurance packages.
-- PARIS CANVASSES BANKS ON SALE OF CREDIT LYONNAIS

The French government is reported to have begun inquiries among leading European banks to discover whether it might be possible to sell the troubled state-controlled Credit Lyonnais banking group. Banks, including Barclays, have been contacted by French government advisers Goldman Sachs. It is thought that the feedback has been that such a sale would not be possible with Credit Lyonnais in its current form. A slimmer operation might prove more saleable, however.
-- CREDIT CARD GROUP SET FOR CONTROL OF MONDEX

The credit card group MasterCard International is reported to have acquired a majority stake in the UK electronic finance company Mondex International. Mondex is a developer of electronic cards that can be charged up with 'cash' and used for making even the smallest of purchases. The company was initially established by the National Westminster and Midland banks, though is now owned by a consortium of 17. The deal will result in MasterCard taking a 51 percent share of the group.
-- US CHIP INDEX SET TO BE AXED

It is reported that there are plans to scrap the book-to-bill ratio, a key indicator in the US of demand for semiconductors. A number of major players in the sector, including Texas Instruments and Intel, have been calling for the abolition for some time, believing that it fails to provide a true indicator of the health of the industry. At present the index covers only US manufacturers, ignoring the sales of major Japanese and South Korean companies.
-- BRITISH GAS FACES 80 MILLION STG BILL FOR SYSTEM FAILURE

British Gas is reported to be facing a bill of 80 million stg arising from problems associated with a new computerised national billing system. Systems failures meant that sales staff were often being left with blank screens while trying to deal with customer enquiries and also resulted in customers being sent the wrong or inflated bills. As a result the company was forced to take on additional staff and embark on an expensive upgrade of the system.
-- EUROPEAN PENSIONS CLAIM ATTACKED

A group of pro-European politicians, including Lord Howe, have attacked recent allegations that Britain will be faced with massive bills to meet the cost of pensions in other EU states if it goes ahead with joining the single currency. Writing in a letter to the Financial Times, they stress that a provision of the Maastricht treaty ensures that national debt remains the sole responsibility of individual EU member states.
-- SCHEME TO MAKE JOBLESS SEEK WORK EXPANDS

The government is to extend a scheme that will force the long-term unemployed to take on work. Project Work, which already operates in two pilot projects will be expanded to cover 30 areas. Although the scheme has failed to result in more than 10 percent of those involved actually finding jobs, it has resulted in large numbers stopping claiming benefits, leading to the conclusion that it is an effective way of dealing with fraudulent claims.
-- FOOD INDUSTRY URGED TO ACT ON 6 BILLION STG TRADE DEFICIT

A study by Strathclyde University concludes that there is considerable scope for improved efficiencies in the UK's food industry, which could go some way to reducing the trade deficit of 6 billion sterling that exists in the sector. The survey, sponsored by food retailer Safeway, also calls for improved cooperation between producers and retailers in an effort to boost the share held by British manufacturers of the British domestic market.
